displayQuote: Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists

meta.title: Who really said "Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — George W. Bush said it verbatim in his 20 Sept 2001 Address to a Joint Session of Congress. Not to be confused with his later ‘with us or against us’ line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: George W. Bush, Address to a Joint Session of Congress, 20 Sept 2001 — nine days after 9/11. The full story and the line it gets confused with.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: Born 6 July 1946 · 43rd President of the United States (2001–2009)
answer.sourceLine: Bush said this verbatim in his Address to a Joint Session of Congress on 20 September 2001, nine days after the September 11 attacks. The full sentence — “Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists” — appears in the official White House transcript.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Address to a Joint Session of Congress and the American People
U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C., nine days after the 9/11 attacks

source.excerpt: And we will pursue nations that provide aid or safe haven to terrorism. Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists. From this day forward, any nation that continues to harbor or support terrorism will be regarded by the United States as a hostile regime.
trail: The official White House transcript records the exact sentence in the speech Bush delivered on 20 September 2001.

Wikipedia’s article on the formulation confirms Bush used these words in his address to Congress and traces the “with us or against us” rhetorical device back through Lenin, Mussolini and the Gospels.

A separate, later Bush line — “You’re either with us or against us in the fight against terror” — comes from a 6 November 2001 news conference with President Chirac, and is frequently blended with the September line.

author.bio: George Walker Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States from 2001 to 2009. His presidency was defined by the response to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, which launched the “War on Terror,” the invasion of Afghanistan, and the 2003 Iraq War. This line, delivered to Congress nine days after 9/11, became one of the most quoted — and most debated — sentences of his tenure.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — but often garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bush is correct. The confusion is over which words he used, and whether the idea was his.

items.who: “You’re either with us or against us”
items.why: Bush did say a “with us or against us” version — but at a 6 November 2001 news conference with Jacques Chirac, not in the September address. People routinely merge the two into a single half-remembered line.

The either/or framing long predates Bush: “Whoever is not with me is against me” appears in Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23, and versions were used by Lenin and Mussolini. Bush’s phrasing was his own, but the rhetorical move was ancient.

misattribution.truthLine: The specific sentence — “Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists” — is authentically Bush’s, spoken in his 20 September 2001 address to Congress.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Delivered nine days after the September 11 attacks, the line put every government on notice that neutrality would be treated as complicity. It became the rhetorical cornerstone of the “War on Terror” and framed the coalition-building that led to the invasion of Afghanistan.

Critics seized on it as a textbook false dilemma — erasing any middle ground — while supporters saw a necessary clarity in a moment of crisis. Either way, it defined the tone of U.S. foreign policy for a decade.
